To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the extent and duration of unloaded cell shortenings in rat ventricular muscle are regulated by the sarcolemmal exchange of Na(+) and Ca(2+).
The Na‐Ca exchanger is the primary determinant of the diastolic membrane‐potential‐dependent inactivation of contraction in isolated rat ventricle cells.
Na‐Ca2 exchange is a voltage‐sensitive, Ca‐release mechanism in ventricular myocytes and is regulated by the rate of membrane repolarization.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the regulation of unloaded cell shorten- ing in isolated rat ventricu- lar myocytes.
the role of the Na(+)-Ca2+ exchangers (NCX1) in the heart and the regulation of the NCX1 by the membrane potential and the intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
the regulation of unloaded cell shorten ing by sarcolemal sodium‐calcium (Na(+)‐Ca(2+)) exchange.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Na(+)‐ Ca2+ exchange in rat ventricular muscle is voltage sensitive, and this voltage sensitivity is the main determinant of contraction in rat ventricular tissue.
the Na-Ca exchanger in the rat ventricular myocyte is voltage sensitive and is responsible for a large part of the Ca2+ entry during the action potential.
the Na-Ca exchange system is a very important factor for the regulation of Ca2+ homeostasis in the cell and thus of the contractility in heart muscle cells.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we showed that Na-Ca exchange can modulate contraction of isolated rat ventricular cells.
the sodium‐calcium exchanger is an important regulator of cardiac contractile function and that the effects are mediated by changes in intracellular calcium levels.
Na+/Ca2+ exchangers (NCX) are important for regulating the intracellular calcium concentration and thus for controlling contraction and relaxation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Na/Ca exchanger can be regulated by membrane potential.
the Na/Ca exchanger is a major player in the control of cardiac muscle contraction and relaxation.
Na-Ca exchange is a major determinant of the inotropism of the heart, and the regulation of this process is complex and involves multiple mechanisms.
